An ancient floodgate built by a lost civilization to control the tides of the [[Great Deep]]. Now half-buried in silt and coral, it is said to lead to passages beneath the sea and into forgotten halls where the [[Drownlight]] still burns.

> [!legend]
> Sailors speak of a hum that rises from the depths on still nights — a sound like voices, or a city dreaming.

## Architecture

- Massive stone arches encrusted with coral and black algae
- Gate mechanisms of unknown metal, engraved with wave-like glyphs
- Faint blue glow emanates from cracks in the stone at low tide

## Current State

The upper courtyard is accessible at low tide, which is when [[Mira Veynn]] first reaches it in [[Into the Undercity]]. The inner passage is blocked by a collapsed portcullis. Strange marine growth reacts to light.

veynn.title: World: Veynn

blocks.text: The last standing city of the Drowned Coast — a vertical sprawl of terraces, bell towers, and salt-stained marble stacked above its own sunken districts. Above: council law. stories.name: The Last City of Veynn
stories.sub: Epic Fantasy · Dark & Gritty · Third Limited

book.label: PART ONE
intro: They say the city drowned twice: once in water, once in the forgetting. Every ledger, every oath, every debt was rewritten by the survivors — which is to say, by the liars.
— from the Harbor Annals, author unrecorded
I have kept the ninth bell silent for nineteen years. Tonight it rings, and I find I cannot remember whether I am its keeper or its prisoner. — journal of the Watcher of the Sunken Gate, final entry

paras: Mira Veynn had counted the bells of the upper city for nineteen years, and never once had they rung at dusk. Tonight they rang nine times, slow and uneven, like a hand unsure of its own strength.

From the watchtower window she saw the harbor lanterns gutter in a wind that did not touch the flags. Somewhere below, in the salt-dark of the lower quarter, a summons was waiting for her with her name misspelled and her fate spelled exactly right.
By morning the rumor had grown teeth. The Watcher of the Sunken Gate had gone silent, and the Council pretended not to notice, which is how Mira knew it mattered.
She traded her cloak for a worse one, her name for no name at all, and went down into the streets where the city kept its honest business — the kind that never saw daylight and never lied about it.
Kael dealt cards the way other men made confessions — slowly, and only when cornered. "Passage through Ward Violet costs more than coin," he said. "It costs a favor. And favors compound."
Mira slid the brass token across the table. His smile faltered for exactly one heartbeat, which from Kael was as good as a scream.

The stairwell yawned like a throat carved into the belly of the city. Damp air rolled up from below, thick with the smell of rot, smoke, and something metallic — like old coins left too long in a gutter.
Kael tightened his hood and signaled for Mira to move first.
"Stay close," he whispered. "The Undercity doesn’t just swallow the unwary. It forgets them."

Mira’s lantern cast a trembling circle of light across the slick stone steps. Water dripped from unseen pipes somewhere below, each drop echoing like a slow heartbeat. The deeper they descended, the more the sound of the surface faded — until the city above was nothing but a memory.

At the bottom, the passage opened into a maze of narrow alleys and stacked walkways. Tattered awnings hung between leaning buildings. Strange sigils glowed faintly on walls. Vendors called out in languages Kael didn’t recognize.
A boy darted past them, barefoot, clutching a stolen loaf. A guard laughed and let him go.
"You were right," Mira murmured. "This place has its own rules."
Kael nodded. Somewhere in this sprawl was the Smuggler’s Broker — and the map fragment they needed to reach the Sunken Gate.
Finding it would be the easy part. Getting out would be another story.
The Broker’s map ended at a door that was not on any map, which Mira decided was either very good or very fatal.
Beyond it, stone gave way to older stone, and the air began to hum — low and patient, like a city dreaming with its eyes open.
Ward Violet did not exist. Everyone agreed on this, especially the people who lived there.
Its lamps burned violet-blue against ordinance, its walls carried messages that rearranged themselves by morning, and its loyalty belonged to whoever remembered the old names.
The first tremor came at low tide. The second came with a sound no one could describe without whispering.
In the lower caverns, the drownlight — steady for eight hundred years — began, very slowly, to blink.
The Gate had waited under the sea for longer than the city had a name, and it recognized her.
That was the part no one had warned Mira about — not that the seal could break, but that it would be glad.
Veynn burned its lanterns one final time, all of them, every window and every wall — not as a signal of surrender, but so the deep would see exactly who it was dealing with.
Fire or heart of Veynn. In the end, the choice was the same choice it had always been.

stories.name: The Ninth Bell
stories.sub: Novella · Same world, forty years earlier · Third Limited

book.label: PART ONE
intro: Before the nine bells there were eight, and before the eight there was a woman who could not sleep for the silence.

paras: Ysolde Veynn counted the bells of the upper city because her mother had, and because there were eight of them, and eight was a number that had never sat right with her. Eight left a gap at dusk where the tide turned and nothing marked it.

The Council had a name for the gap. They called it the Quiet Hour and pretended it was a courtesy to the dead. Ysolde, who had spent forty years listening to it, knew a held breath when she heard one.
The bell-foundry had been drowned with the rest of the lower city and had gone on working anyway, in the way of Veynn, on a schedule no one above admitted to keeping.
She found the bellwright by the light of his own furnace, casting nothing, waiting. "You’re late," he said. "By about nineteen years."
A bell, the bellwright said, is a memory with a tongue. You do not cast it. You persuade it. And the ninth bell had been persuaded once already, long ago, by whoever had built the Gate.
Ysolde touched the cold mould and felt, faintly, the sea on the other side of it, listening.
The Council forbade the casting in the usual manner — politely, in writing, with a fine attached and a second fine for reading the first one aloud.
Ysolde paid both and had the receipt framed. Her daughter, who was two, would grow up thinking this was how all women dealt with councils. In Veynn, she would be right.

It rang once. The tide turned. Somewhere very far down, a gate that had waited under the sea for longer than the city had a name heard its own voice for the first time in eight hundred years, and answered.
Ysolde, on the bell stair with her daughter on her hip, felt the answer through the stone and understood — too late, and exactly on time — what she had done.
They made her the bell’s keeper, since she was the one who had woken it. Nineteen years, they said, and then it would be someone else’s. She looked at the child on her hip and said nothing.
The Watcher of the Sunken Gate wrote one line in his journal that night: it will be the daughter. He did not write which one he was afraid for.

rite.title: The Hollow Rite

blocks.text: When a sovereign of Caerwyn dies, the body is hollowed, dressed, and seated on the next empty terrace of [[Caerwyn Keep]]. The rite takes seven days and seven cuts. A hollowed king is said to retain one thing: the ability to refuse. No one alive has heard a refusal. [[Queen Maelis]] has declined the rite for herself twice, in writing.

blocks.title: The question the books turn on

book.label: PART ONE
intro: Forty kings sit beneath Caerwyn. Every dawn a man counts them. Every dawn the number is the same. This is the entire constitution of the realm.
— from the Wardens’ Primer, third edition

paras: Teodric Vale had counted the kings of Caerwyn every dawn for twenty years, and the number had never once been interesting. Forty. Forty seated, forty silent, forty crowned in bone and dressed in the colours they had died in.

On the ninth day of Ashfall he counted forty, and then, because the light on the third terrace fell wrong, he counted again. Forty. He wrote it in the ledger. He did not write that the thirty-first king had turned his head.

A warden’s ledger records numbers, not observations. Teodric had been told this on his first day by a man who was now seated on the fifth terrace, and he had believed it for two decades because believing it was restful.
He turned the ledger to a fresh page and wrote, in the margin where no one looked: he is facing the door now.
"You are the one who counts," said Queen Maelis, and Teodric understood that she had not asked a question, and that he was expected to answer it anyway.
"Every dawn, Majesty." "And are they all still there?" He thought of the thirty-first king. "Every one of them is exactly where he was placed," he said, which was true of thirty-nine.

Lord Casimir Dray spoke for the kings the way a tide speaks for the moon: constantly, and without permission. "The crypt is silent on the matter of the grain levy," he announced, "and silence is assent."
The Bone Court murmured. Teodric, standing where wardens stood, looked at his boots and thought about which door the thirty-first king was facing, and what was on the other side of it.
The morning the count came to thirty-nine, Teodric stood on the third terrace for a long time with the ledger open and the pen dry.
The thirty-first chair was not empty. It was occupied by exactly what had always occupied it. But the king who had sat there was, in some way Teodric had no word for, no longer in attendance.
Dray wanted the ledger. The Queen wanted the truth. Teodric wanted, with a purity that surprised him, to have been born a farmer.
He gave the Queen the ledger and Dray the truth, and discovered that in Caerwyn those were the same betrayal.
The kings had always been able to refuse. Everyone knew it the way everyone knew the mountain was tall — as a fact that required nothing of them.
What no one had considered was what forty refusals at once would sound like, or that the sound would be a door.

book.label: LETTERS I–IX
intro: Aurel — I have numbered these so you will know when one is missing. I have also lied about the numbers, so you will not know how many. Forgive me both.

scenes.t: The Sea Is Nothing Like They Told Us
paras: Aurel — The sea is nothing like they told us. It does not roar. It sighs, all day, like a bored courtier, and then at night it comes up the shingle and takes things: a boot, a bucket, the Queen’s second-best chair.
She is well. If you can call this well. She sits on the first-best chair and watches the water and says, every evening, "It never asks," and I write it down because that is what I am for.

The boat comes twice a season. The man who rows it will not take letters addressed to the Keep, so this is addressed to a bone-warden’s apprentice at a mountain, which is where you live, and is not the Keep, and he is satisfied.
I have put a shell in with this one. It is not for you. It is proof that I am somewhere.

You asked what Teodric Vale told me the night the count broke. I took it down in shorthand; here is the long hand. He said the kings had turned. He said all of them. He said it the way you used to report the weather — embarrassed to be the one bringing it.
Then he asked me to spell his name correctly in the record, because he expected to be seated soon and wanted the plaque right. I spelled it correctly. He is not seated. Nor, I think, will he be.
I have taken work in the sheds. The Guild pays in salt, which is funny until you try to buy bread with it. The Queen has taken work too, and will not say where, and comes back smelling of tar.
The sea took another chair last night. We are running out of chairs, Aurel, and I am beginning to think that is the point.
Your reply came wet and three seasons late, and I have dried it on a rock and read it eleven times and I am not going to answer the question in it, because you already know.
Yes. She would go back. Yes. I would go with her. No. Neither of us will say so aloud, because the sea is listening, and the sea never asks, and I have grown to love that about it.
There is one chair left. She has given it to the water on purpose — walked it down the shingle at low tide and set it facing the mountain and come back with her skirts soaked and her face dry.
"Let them count that," she said. I wrote it down. I always write it down. This is letter the fourteenth, and it is the twelfth.

events.d: [[Ilse Marrow]] writes from [[Greywater]]. The sea is nothing like they told us.
The boat comes twice a season. A shell as proof of somewhere.
The night the count broke, retold — [[Teodric Vale]]’s testimony in long hand.
[[Queen Maelis]] takes work and will not say where. Chairs are running out.
Walked into the sea at low tide, facing the mountain. Let them count that.

detail.sum: Maelis gives the last chair to the water. Ilse writes it down: letter the fourteenth, and it is the twelfth.

l1.label: The Sea Is Nothing Like They Told Us

crafterDraftVeynn: The door was not on any map, and it knew it. Mira ran her palm along the seam where stone met older stone, and the hum rose to meet her — low, patient, familiar in a way that made her stomach drop.
Behind her, Kael laughed at something the patrol sergeant said, too loud and half a beat too late. He was buying her seconds and spending them badly.
“Open, then,” she whispered — not to the door, but to the blood that already knew the way. The seam breathed. Somewhere below, the drownlight blinked.

Smuggler — witty, guarded, survivor.
Antagonist — elusive, always watching.
Drowned streets, stacked walkways.

Redraws itself at low tide.
Burns underwater. Misbehaves near flame.
The rules by which the deep breathes.
